cards.title: The internet makes no promises
cards.body:
Here's a surprise: the Internet [[Protocol]] **doesn't promise** that [[packets|packet]] arrive in order. It doesn't even promise they arrive at all.

Yet when you download a photo, it shows up perfectly, every single time. In this lesson you'll see how the internet turns an unreliable journey into a reliable delivery.

cards.title: Routes can change
cards.body:
[[Routers|router]] keep updating their [[routing tables|routing-table]]. If a connection breaks, or gets very busy, they find another way round.

So the route can change partway through a conversation. Most of the time a conversation's [[packets|packet]] all follow the same road, but when the route changes, packets that took different roads can arrive in a **different order** from the one they were sent in.

cards.prompt: The cable from **Router A** straight to the web [[server]] has been cut, so it's no longer on the map. Get the [[packet]] to the **web server** another way.
cards.explanation: Either detour works: through **Router B**, or through **Router A** and on to **Router C**. A broken cable doesn't stop the whole internet, because routers simply send packets another way. But if some packets take one road and some take the other, they may arrive in a different order.
cards.hint: The cut cable is gone from the map, so only follow the links you can see. There's more than one way round.
cards.nudge: Check that every step follows a line on the map. The link from [[Router]] A straight to the server has been removed.

cards.prompt: These packets arrived jumbled up. Use their **sequence numbers** to put them back in order.
cards.explanation: Sorting by sequence number gives **#1, #2, #3, #4**: *PACKETS CAN ARRIVE JUMBLED*. The receiver doesn't care what order packets turn up in. The sequence numbers say where each piece belongs.
cards.hint: Ignore the words for a moment and look at the number after the # on each packet.
cards.nudge: Sort by the number after the #, from smallest to largest. The order they arrived in doesn't matter.

cards.prompt: [[Packets|packet]] arrive in the order **2, 1, 3**. What does the receiving computer do?

options.text: Uses the sequence numbers to put them back as 1, 2, 3
Uses them in the order they arrived: 2, 1, 3
options.nudge: Using packets in the order they turned up would scramble the data. Think about what the sequence numbers are for.

options.text: Throws them all away and asks for everything again
options.nudge: Nothing is wrong with these packets, and none are missing. They just arrived in a different order.

options.text: Asks the sender to send them in the right order next time
options.nudge: The sender can't control which road each packet takes, and the receiver doesn't need it to.

cards.explanation: Every packet carries its **sequence number**, so the receiver simply puts them back as 1, 2, 3. Using them as they arrived would scramble your data. And nothing is wrong with the packets, so there's no need to throw them away or send them again.
cards.hint: Every packet carries a sequence number. How could the receiver use it when packets turn up jumbled?

cards.title: Missing packets and TCP
cards.body:
Sometimes a [[packet]] never arrives. A [[router]] that's too busy might have to drop it, or interference on Wi-Fi might scramble it.

For things like web pages, photos and downloads, computers follow a set of rules called **TCP**, short for **Transmission Control [[Protocol]]**. TCP is the partner set of rules that adds the [[sequence numbers|sequence-number]]. The receiver keeps telling the sender which packets have arrived. If there's a gap in the sequence numbers, the sender sends the missing packet again.

Put together, IP gets packets across the internet, and TCP makes sure they all arrive and end up in the right order. You'll look closer at TCP in a later module.

cards.prompt: A message was sent as [[packets|packet]] 1 to 6. Packets **1, 2, 3, 5 and 6** arrived. Which packet number needs to be sent again?
cards.explanation: The [[sequence numbers|sequence-number]] jump from 3 to 5, so **packet 4** is missing. Only that one needs to be sent again. The receiver can keep 5 and 6 and slot 4 in when it arrives.
cards.hint: Count along from 1 to 6 and look for the gap in the numbers that arrived.
cards.nudge: List the numbers 1 to 6 and tick off each one that arrived. The one without a tick is the answer.

cards.prompt: Match each problem to how the internet deals with it.
cards.explanation: Out-of-order packets are **sorted** using their sequence numbers. A missing packet is **sent again**, thanks to [[TCP]]. And when a connection breaks, routers [[update]] their tables and **send packets another way**.
cards.hint: Think about which fix uses sequence numbers, which one sends a piece again, and which one is a job for routers.
cards.nudge: Sequence numbers fix order, resending fixes a missing piece, and routers deal with problems along the road.

cards.prompt: On a video call, a lost packet makes the picture glitch for a moment. The call doesn't pause to wait for the packet to be sent again. Why not?

options.text: Waiting would make the call lag. For live video, fresh data is more useful than late data

options.nudge: Everything on the internet travels in packets, video calls included.

options.text: Video packets can never be lost
options.nudge: Any packet can go missing, video ones too. The question says a lost packet caused the glitch.

options.text: Video packets are too big to send twice
options.nudge: Packet size isn't the reason. Think about timing: what happens to a live call while it waits?

cards.explanation: In a live call, a packet that arrives half a second late is useless: that moment has already passed. So live apps usually skip lost packets and keep going, often using a simpler set of rules called **UDP** (User Datagram [[Protocol]]), which doesn't resend anything. A short glitch is better than the whole call freezing. For a download, it's the other way round: every [[byte]] has to be perfect, so [[TCP]] waits and resends.
cards.hint: In a live call, what's the use of a picture from half a second ago that turns up late?

cards.prompt: Yesterday's [[traceroute]] to example.com is saved at the top of the [[terminal]]. Run `traceroute example.com` now and compare the two, [[hop]] by hop (the numbered lines). One hop has changed.
cards.intro:
Saved from yesterday:

$ traceroute example.com
traceroute to example.com (198.51.100.10), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  192.168.1.1 (192.168.1.1)  1.912 ms  1.804 ms  1.765 ms
 2  203.0.113.1 (203.0.113.1)  9.483 ms  9.412 ms  9.377 ms
 3  203.0.113.65 (203.0.113.65)  11.207 ms  11.164 ms  11.122 ms
 4  198.51.100.1 (198.51.100.1)  18.930 ms  18.842 ms  19.004 ms
 5  example.com (198.51.100.10)  19.315 ms  19.271 ms  19.233 ms

Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.description: List each router between you and example.com, right now

success.question: What is the address of the router that's on today's route but wasn't on yesterday's?

cards.explanation: Hop 3 was `203.0.113.65` yesterday and is `203.0.113.129` today. Every other hop is the same. Maybe the old [[router]] was busy or being repaired, so traffic was sent another way. The detour is a little slower (about 22 ms to the end instead of 19 ms), but your [[packets|packet]] still get there.
cards.hint: Run `traceroute example.com`, then compare the address on each numbered line with yesterday's, one line at a time.
cards.nudge: The times change a little on every line, so compare only the addresses. Give the address that appears today, not yesterday's.

cards.title: Recap: Packets and Routing
cards.body:
- Data travels in **packets**, each with addresses and a **sequence number** added.
- **Routers** pass packets [[hop]] by hop, using their [[routing tables|routing-table]]. **Traceroute** shows the hops.
- Routes can **change**, so packets may arrive out of order. Some may go missing.
- **TCP** puts packets back in order and gets missing ones sent again. Some live apps, like video calls, skip lost packets instead of waiting for them.

Take the module quiz to finish Packets and Routing.
